title: Step Track
context: Grade 4, and the chapter's central skill: carrying a series on by finding its rule. An adult sees next terms being written. What is actually being practised is checking the step between every pair of neighbours rather than only the first, which is the only way to notice that one of the six printed patterns on the exercise page has no fixed step at all. The rule maker also answers the opening page's closing task, create a number sequence of your own, which the Concept Linking box two pages later sends the child back to.

writeup.why: Find the step from each term to the next, check it all along, and carry a number or letter series on, or make one of your own from a start and a rule.
writeup.look: A track of stepping stones with a jump arc over every pair of neighbours, a letter track under it, and a pairing tray and a rule maker at the side.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Step Track' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the stones filled against the stones this phase leaves blank, two numbers in ink. The first climbs by one as each stone fills or each heap is paired, and the second is fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score, even on a track that does. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. Stepping stones run across the working area: ten stones, each 96 across with 12 between, at 64,300, reaching 1132. Over every pair of neighbours hangs a jump arc, in the band from 222 to 292, with its label sitting on the arc itself. The step finder fills the labels one at a time from the left, each as the second term less the first. A step up is labelled with an add sign and a step down with a take-away sign. Arc compare lifts any two arcs and stands them side by side in a box 140 by 90 at 600,630, where a difference in length is seen at once. A counting-down track is laid from the right, so it runs towards a zero stone at its left end with nothing drawn beyond it. A step that would pass zero is handed back with the zero stone lit in reddish purple. The letter track runs under the number track: twenty-six small stones, each 38 across with 3 between, at 64,450, reaching 1127. Its own arcs hang in the band from 406 to 446, and the place toggle writes each letter's place in the alphabet in the row from 492 to 516. The pairing tray sits at the lower left, 520 by 190 at 64,530, and takes a heap of up to twenty counters. Pair them sets the counters out two by two at walking pace. Any counter left without a partner stands on its own at the end, in reddish purple. The even or odd card, 140 by 90 at 600,530, turns from what is left. The rule maker sits at the lower right, 400 by 190 at 750,530, and takes a start, or two starts, and one rule from its list. The list holds four rules: add a step, take a step away, add each number to itself, and add the two numbers before. The track then fills stone by stone with every arc labelled as it lands. On the last two rules each new arc is drawn up out of the stones it came from. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a term or a step is asked for, with an add key and a take-away key beside them. On the letter track it becomes twenty-six letter keys, seven across in four rows, with the last row holding five. The even and odd keys stand under both, and on the fourth phase the rule maker's four rules are keys of their own. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Whatever the stage hands over is deep blue: a given term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter, a tile already laid. The first member of a repeating group is deep blue too, and the second member, or a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself is vermilion in every tool without exception: a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, an operation sign, a key's shift. Whatever the rule makes is green: a next term, a built box, a coded or decoded letter, a copy just laid, a tick. Whatever the child is asked to notice is reddish purple: a broken box, a closed-in gap, a doubled part, a leftover counter, a line put back. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome. Chrome never borrows a content colour, and no content colour is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a thing is told by its label or its place before it is told by its colour. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. No track is ever drawn running on past its zero stone, and no stone, label or dot is drawn to the left of it. A list printed with dots after its last term says the list goes on, and on this stage a count down that has reached zero has nowhere left to go.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last track the child filled with every jump arc labelled, and the series they built in the rule maker standing under it with its start and its rule written beside it.

phases.win: every arc shows the same label and the blank stones fill one jump at a time
phases.does: labels every arc with the step, checks that they match, then fills the blank stones
phases.goal: the step between neighbours is found, checked all along and used, and a count down stops at zero
phases.says: How far is each jump? Check every one before you go on.
phases.check: Away from the screen: count down from forty in steps of ten. Say the last number, and why it is the last.
phases.feels: every jump the same size, checked all along, and a count down that has somewhere to stop
phases.hands: Chalk a trail of squares in the playground. One child sets a start and a secret step and chalks the first four terms. The next child walks the trail, says the step between every pair aloud, and chalks the next three. Then chalk a trail that counts down by eight from fifty-six, and ask what the last square holds and why nothing comes after it. Counting back in ones is called counting back; use no other name for it.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what is the jump between the first two stones? Second rung, the phase's: is it the same between every pair? Third rung: the track is cut to three stones and one blank, and the child labels both arcs before filling it. The number keys stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the first two terms are the first thing read, and on most tracks the first step is the only step there is.
wrong.move: reads the step off the first pair and carries it on without checking the pairs after it.
wrong.screen: the step finder labels every arc again one at a time from the left, and any arc whose label differs is ringed in reddish purple. The child's stones stay where they were filled. Arc compare stands that arc beside the first, and both stay on the stage.

wrong.why: the list that goes down by fifty ends in dots after fifty, and dots say that a list goes on.
wrong.move: carries a count down on past the zero stone, or stops at the last term printed before it.
wrong.screen: a step that would pass zero is handed back with the zero stone lit, and nothing is drawn to the left of it. Where the child stopped short, the stone before zero stays drawn and open. The count down is then walked from the first term, one jump at a time, to zero, where it stops.

phases.screen: a number track with four terms written and three stones blank, its jump arcs unlabelled
phases.soWhat: Find the step between neighbours, check it for every pair, then keep using it; a count down stops at zero.

phases.win: the next letters light on the track, each with its place in the alphabet beneath it
phases.does: counts the places between neighbouring letters, then steps on by the same amount
phases.goal: letters step along the alphabet the way numbers step along counting
phases.says: How many letters does it jump? Jump the same again.
phases.check: Write the next two letters of C, F, I, and say each one's place in the alphabet.
phases.feels: letters line up like numbers, each with its own place, and a jump along them is counted by its landings
phases.hands: Write the alphabet in a long line across the board and number each letter under it from one. Ask the class to jump from A three letters at a time, touching each landing letter with a ruler and counting the jumps, not the letters passed over. Then write B two, D four, F six, and ask what the numbers have to do with the letters.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many landings from one letter to the next? Second rung, the phase's: what is that letter's place in the alphabet? Third rung: the track is cut to its first ten letters, and the child jumps once with the landings counted aloud. The letter keys stay open.

wrong.why: between A and D there are two letters to see, B and C, and seeing them is easier than counting landings.
wrong.move: counts the letters in between instead of the jump, so A to D reads as a step of two and the track goes on J, L, N.
wrong.screen: the letter track counts the jump from A one landing at a time, lighting B, then C, then D, and numbering each landing. The count stops on the letter it lands on, at three. The child's letters stay on their stones, and the same count is run again from J.

wrong.why: the number step is plain to read, and the letter step is hidden by the letters in between.
wrong.move: steps the letter and its number by different amounts, writing I ten after H eight.
wrong.screen: the place toggle writes each letter's place beneath it, and the child's I stands with nine beneath it, not ten. The jump from H is then counted landing by landing to J, and J's place is written under it. Both letters stay on the track.

phases.screen: the letter track with four letters lit and three places waiting
phases.soWhat: Letters step along the alphabet the way numbers step along counting, and each letter has its place, A as one.

phases.win: the pairs line up and the card turns, with any leftover counter standing on its own
phases.does: sets the counters out two by two and turns the card from what is left
phases.goal: a number that pairs up with none left over is even, and one that leaves one over is odd
phases.says: Put them in pairs. Is anyone left without a partner?
phases.check: Away from the screen: take a handful of beans and put them in pairs. Is your handful even or odd?
phases.feels: the counters line up two by two, and either everyone has a partner or one is left on its own
phases.hands: Hand each pair a heap of buttons, some heaps even and some odd in number. Ask them to set the buttons out two by two, and not to count them first. Then ask whether anyone is left without a partner. Write the counts on the board in two lists, and ask what the class notices about the numbers in each list.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many pairs did the counters make? Second rung, the phase's: is any counter left without a partner? Third rung: the heap is cut to five counters, and the child pairs them one pair at a time. The even and odd keys stay open.

wrong.why: making pairs felt like the whole job, and five pairs were made without any trouble.
wrong.move: calls eleven even because five pairs could be made, without looking at the button left over.
wrong.screen: the pairing tray sets the counters out again two by two at walking pace, and the one left over stands apart at the end in reddish purple. The card waits face down until the leftover has been tapped. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: a number is read from the left, and the one is the first thing the eye lands on.
wrong.move: calls fourteen odd because its first digit, one, is odd.
wrong.screen: fourteen counters are paired, first a ten making five pairs with none over, then the four making two pairs with none over. Seven pairs stand in a row with no counter left alone. The child's card stays beside the tray.

phases.screen: the pairing tray holding a heap of counters, with an even or odd card waiting
phases.soWhat: A number that pairs up with none left over is even, and one that leaves one over is odd.

phases.win: the next stone fills and its arc is drawn out of the number already reached
phases.does: reads what each step is, fills the next stone, then builds a series of their own from a start and a rule
phases.goal: when the steps are not equal each step is looked at, and a start and a rule make a series of your own
phases.says: The jumps are not the same. Where does each jump come from?
phases.check: Five, ten, twenty, forty. Say where each step comes from, and what comes next.
phases.feels: the jumps grow, and each one is exactly as big as the number the series has already reached
phases.hands: Write six, twelve, twenty-four, forty-eight on the board and ask for the step. Let the class find that the steps are not equal before anyone says why. Then ask where each step comes from, and lay out twelve counters and twelve more to make twenty-four. Each number is added to itself, which is addition the class already has, so name no new rule for it. Finish on the opening page's own task: every child makes a sequence of their own and says its start and its rule.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: are the jumps the same? Second rung, the phase's: how big is each jump next to the stone it starts from? Third rung: the track is cut to two stones and one blank, and the child lays the first stone's counters along the jump. The number keys and the rule list stay open.

wrong.why: the summary box on the same page says number patterns are made by skip counting, and every pattern in the section before this one kept a fixed step.
wrong.move: calls the pattern skip counting and adds the last step again, writing seventy-two after forty-eight.
wrong.screen: the step finder labels the three arcs six, twelve and twenty-four, and arc compare stands them side by side, plainly not equal. Each arc is then drawn up out of the stone it starts from, as long as that stone's number. The child's seventy-two stays on its stone.

wrong.why: the start is the one number that stays in view the whole time, and adding it again looks like keeping to a rule.
wrong.move: in a series of their own made by adding the two numbers before, adds each new number to the start instead, so three, four, seven goes on to ten.
wrong.screen: the rule maker draws two arcs into each new stone, one from each of the two stones before it. The child's ten stands on its stone with its own two arcs, from the start and from the seven. The rule maker's stone lands beside it with its arcs from the four and the seven.

phases.screen: a track whose jump arcs carry different labels, with the rule maker open beside it
phases.soWhat: When the steps are not equal, look at what each step is: here each number is added to itself.
phases.concept: When the steps are not equal

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when a stone fills on a track whose steps are not equal. The number already reached lifts off its stone as a rod of counters, and a copy of the rod lays itself along the next jump, where it fits exactly. The next stone lands at the rod's far end with its number written on it. On a track built in the rule maker from two starts, the rod lifts from the stone two back instead, and fits the jump just as exactly. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a number track stands with four terms written, three stones blank and every jump arc unlabelled. On the second the letter track stands with four letters lit and three places waiting. On the third the pairing tray holds a heap of counters, with the even or odd card face down beside it. On the fourth a track stands whose arcs already carry labels that differ, with the rule maker open at the lower right. The running count at the top left holds the stones filled against the stones this phase leaves blank, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first unlabelled arc, or the first letter, or the heap, or the largest label, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how far each jump goes. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any start and any rule in the rule maker, on the number track or the letter track, with the pairing tray open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the step between neighbours, letters that step, pairing for even and odd, and series whose steps are not equal, including one the child makes from a start and a rule.
voiceLines: A track of stones, with a jump between each pair. How far is every jump?
How far is each jump? Check every one before you go on.
How many letters does it jump? Jump the same again.
Put them in pairs. Is anyone left without a partner?
The jumps are not the same. Where does each jump come from?
Another track. Check every jump before you fill a stone.
Free play. Choose a start and a rule, and watch the track fill.
Label each jump again from the left, and look for the one that differs.
Every jump labelled, and every series carried on by its own rule.

observations.why: Labels written between every pair of neighbours can be read along the track like a row of their own.
observations.soWhat: Check the step between every pair, not only the first, before carrying a series on.
observations.observe: The step finder labelled every arc, and the one that differed stood out without being looked for.

observations.why: Among the numbers the class counts with, there is nothing below zero to step on to.
observations.soWhat: A series that counts down stops at zero.
observations.observe: The count down reached the zero stone and the next step was handed back.

observations.why: Pairing takes two at a time, so a heap either uses every counter or leaves exactly one over.
observations.soWhat: A number that pairs with none left over is even, and one that leaves one over is odd.
observations.observe: Eleven counters made five pairs, and one counter stood on its own.

observations.why: Each step was the number already reached, so each number was added to itself.
observations.soWhat: When the steps are not equal, look at where each step comes from before guessing the next one.
observations.observe: The arcs of the last track were not equal, and each one was as long as the stone it started from.

source_tool.description: A track of stepping stones runs across the stage with a term written on each stone and the last few stones blank. Over every pair of neighbours hangs a jump arc with an empty label, and a step finder fills each label by taking one term from the next, so a series whose step is the same all along shows the same label on every arc, and one whose steps differ shows it at once. A step can go up or down. Going down, the track runs towards a zero stone at its left end and stops there: a step that would pass zero is handed back with the zero stone lit. A letter track runs under the number track with the alphabet on its stones, and letters step along it exactly as numbers do, each letter carrying its place in the alphabet beneath it when that is asked for. A pairing tray takes a heap of counters and sets them out two by two, leaving any counter without a partner standing on its own at the end. A rule maker lets the child build a series of their own: pick a start, then pick a rule, add the same step, take the same step away, add each number to itself, or add the two numbers before, and the track fills stone by stone with every arc labelled.
source_tool.art_direction: Stepping stones with a jump over each / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a strip of picture cells, a paper arrow on a dial, stepping stones with jump arcs between them, counters that pair up, a tower of boxes each resting on two below, two rings of letters that turn, a ruled board of sums with a slate beside it, and a bench of dotted paper with a tray of tiles.
A repeating group is always shown whole. When a bracket is drawn over it, every copy of it along the row is lit at once, and a copy that does not match is left unlit rather than hidden.

Every step in a series is drawn as an arc from one term to the next with its label on the arc, never as a bare number between two terms, so the step between every pair of neighbours can be read, not only the first.
A counting-down track has a zero stone at its left end and nothing beyond it. No track, board or list is ever drawn running on past zero.

Every box of a number tower rests visibly on exactly two boxes below it, and the operation sign is drawn between each pair of neighbours in every row, so a tower that keeps to one operation shows the same sign all the way up.
The alphabet is always drawn round a circle, twenty-six letters evenly spaced, so the last letter sits beside the first and no letter ever falls off an end.
A line put back into a board is drawn sliding into its place between its neighbours, and the jump labels either side of it are rewritten where they stand, never cleared.

Tiles are drawn at true relative size, edge to edge where they touch, never overlapping unless the frame is showing an overlap on purpose, and a circle is never squeezed to close a gap. A tile drawn taller than it is wide is never called a square.
A shape, a term or a box is told apart by its label or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a shape, a term, a box, a letter or a tile the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Whatever the stage hands over, a printed term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter of a message and a tile already laid, is deep blue, and so is the first member of a repeating group. The second member of a repeating group, and a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself, a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, the operation sign between two boxes and the shift a key makes from a letter to its partner, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is the rule cannot afford a frame where the step has to be hunted for. Whatever the rule makes, a next term, a box built from the two below it, a coded or decoded letter, a tile carried on and a tick on the can do list, is green. Whatever the child is asked to notice, a box that breaks the tower's operation, a space with tiles closed round it, a part where two tiles lie on top of each other, a counter left without a partner and a missing line put back on a board, is reddish purple. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome, and the outer edge of a tiled patch is traced in that plain line and never filled, because it is where the tiling stops and not a gap. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box and never a faded copy of its answer. All of that holds in greyscale, because a jump label sits on its own arc, a broken box keeps its light on after the check has moved past it, a closed-in gap is filled while the outer edge is only outlined, and a leftover counter stands apart from the pairs.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Label each jump again from the left, and look for the one that differs.
voice.onNext: Another track. Check every jump before you fill a stone.
voice.opening: A track of stones, with a jump between each pair. How far is every jump?
voice.onFinish: Every jump labelled, and every series carried on by its own rule.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Choose a start and a rule, and watch the track fill.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.

phase_map.concept: When the steps are not equal

placement.where: After a chalk trail of numbers has been walked in the playground, and before the printed patterns are opened. The tool is what labels the jump between every pair of neighbours at once, so a step that changes part way along is seen rather than missed, which a pencil working left to right does not show.

answer_key.rule: A series is a list in order and each item in it is a term. To carry one on, find the step from each term to the next and check it between every pair of neighbours, not only the first. A step can add or take away. Counting back in ones is counting back, and a series that counts down stops at zero. Letters step along the alphabet the way numbers step along counting, and each letter has its place, A as one up to Z as twenty-six. A number that pairs up with none left over is even and one that leaves one over is odd, and the counting numbers take turns, odd, even, odd, even. When the steps are not equal, look at what each step is: where each step is the number already reached, each number is added to itself, and where each number is the sum of the two numbers before it, the steps grow as well. A series of your own needs a start and a rule.
answer_key.wrong: The jump arcs are relabelled one at a time from the left, so the arc whose label differs from the rest is found by the child, and the pairing tray sets the counters out two by two again at walking pace. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Find the step between neighbours: 12 is 5 more than 7, and 17 is 5 more than 12.
Check the last pair too: 22 is 5 more than 17, so the step is 5 all along.
items.question: Write the next three terms of 7, 12, 17, 22.
items.checkpoint: Find the step between neighbours, check it holds for every pair, then keep using it.
items.misconception: Checking only the first pair, and so missing a series whose step changes further along.

steps: Each letter is two places on from the one before: B, then D, then F, then H.
The number with each letter is its place in the alphabet, so B is 2 and D is 4.
Two places on from H come J, L and N, the 10th, 12th and 14th letters, so the terms are J10, L12 and N14.
items.question: Write the next three terms of B2, D4, F6, H8.
items.checkpoint: A letter pattern has a step too, counted along the alphabet.
items.misconception: Stepping the letter and the number by different amounts, so the number stops matching the letter's place.

steps: Set the buttons out two by two until no more pairs can be made.
Five pairs use ten buttons, and one button is left without a partner.
A number that leaves one over when it is paired is odd, so eleven is odd.
items.answer: Five pairs with one button left over, so eleven is odd
items.question: Eleven buttons are put into pairs. How many pairs are there, and is eleven even or odd?
items.checkpoint: Even numbers pair up with none left over; odd numbers leave one over.
items.misconception: Calling eleven even because five pairs could be made, without looking at the button left over.

steps: The steps 6, 12 and 24 are not equal, so this series has no fixed step.
Each step is the number the series has already reached: 6 and 6 make 12, 12 and 12 make 24, and 24 and 24 make 48.
So each number is added to itself, and the next term is 48 + 48 = 96.
items.answer: Each step is the number already reached, so 96 comes next
items.question: Look at 6, 12, 24, 48. The steps are 6, 12 and 24. What is each step, and what comes next?
items.checkpoint: When the steps are not equal, look at what each step is.
items.misconception: Adding the last step, 24, again and writing 72.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Write the next three terms of 5, 11, 17, 23.
Write the next four terms of 56, 48, 40, 32, and say what happens after that.
items.final_answer: 24, 16, 8 and 0. The step takes away 8 each time, and the count stops at zero

items.question: Write the next two terms of A, D, G, J.
items.final_answer: M and P, because each letter is three places on from the one before

items.question: Write the next three terms of Y25, V22, S19.
items.final_answer: P16, M13, J10, because each letter goes three places back and its number is its place in the alphabet

items.question: Fourteen socks are put into pairs. Is fourteen even or odd, and how does pairing show it?
items.final_answer: Even, because fourteen socks make seven pairs with none left over

items.question: Write the next three terms of 31, 33, 35, 37, and say whether each term is even or odd.
items.final_answer: 39, 41 and 43. Each is odd, because adding two adds one more pair and the one left over stays

items.question: Write the next two terms of 9, 18, 36, 72.
items.final_answer: 144 and 288. The steps 9, 18 and 36 are not equal. Each step is the number already reached, so each number is added to itself: 72 + 72 = 144 and 144 + 144 = 288

items.question: Make a series of your own that starts 3, 4 and makes each next number by adding the two numbers before it. Write the next four numbers.

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: labels every jump arc with the step between two neighbours
takes the next term and checks it against the step
stops a counting-down track at zero and lights when a step would pass it
steps letters along the alphabet with each letter's place beneath it
sets counters out two by two and stands any leftover on its own
stands two jump arcs side by side to show whether the steps are equal
builds a series from a chosen start and a chosen rule
offers add a step, take a step away, add the number to itself, and add the two before

teaching_notes: Walk a chalk trail of numbers before the tool is opened, one child setting a start and a secret step and the next child finding it. Then insist on checking the step between every pair of neighbours, not only the first two, because that is the one habit the printed exercise needs and does not teach. Five of its six patterns keep a fixed step and a child reading only the first pair gets all five right. The sixth doubles: its steps are not equal and they get bigger. Let the class find that, then ask where each step comes from, and let them see that each step is the number already reached, so each number is added to itself. That is addition. Do not name a new rule for it; the summary box on the same page says patterns are made by skip counting, and the point is that this one is not. The page that introduces number patterns gives counting back in ones a skip counting name; call it counting back. Its list that goes down by fifty ends in dots, and the next term is zero, where the count stops. The opening page's list, each number the sum of the two before it, is never used again in the chapter, and the Concept Linking box sends the class back to it for a question that is not there. Use the rule maker for the opening page's own task instead: every child makes a sequence of their own and says its start and its rule. The book calls a list in order a series; keep its word, since it is one of the four vocabulary words, and say that it means a list.
generation_prompt: Build a series tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A horizontal track of evenly spaced stepping stones runs across the working area, a term written on each stone and the last few stones blank. Over every pair of neighbouring stones hangs a jump arc with an empty label; a step finder fills each label with the difference between the two terms, going up or down, and an arc compare control stands any two arcs side by side. When a track counts down it ends at a zero stone on its left with nothing drawn beyond it, and a step that would pass zero is handed back with the zero stone lit. A letter track runs under the number track with the twenty-six letters on its stones, and a place toggle writes each letter's place in the alphabet beneath it. A pairing tray at one side takes a heap of up to twenty counters and sets them out two by two, standing any counter without a partner on its own at the end, and an even or odd card turns from what is left. A rule maker takes a start, or two starts, and one rule from a list, add a step, take a step away, add each number to itself, or add the two numbers before, and fills the track stone by stone with every arc labelled. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Find the jump between each pair of numbers. Check every jump. Use the same jump to fill the empty stones. Put the counters in pairs. If the jumps are not the same, look at where each jump comes from.
